title: Testing quantum Gaussianity with constant sample complexity
authors: Mahtab Yaghubi Rad, Ricard Puig, Saksham Hassanandani, Luke Coffman, Jens Eisert, Carlos Bravo-Prieto, Antonio Anna Mele
abstract: Efficiently testing whether a quantum state possesses a given structure is both a fundamental and a practical task in quantum information. Among the most important structured families are Gaussian states, which underpin quantum optics and many-body physics while defining paradigmatic regimes of efficient classical simulation. Despite the central role of Gaussian states, optimal tests of Gaussianity have remained unknown. Here we give optimal and robust algorithms for testing fermionic and bosonic Gaussian states, with sample complexity independent of system size, particle number, and energy. Remarkably, the protocols implement experimentally feasible measurements associated with known exact symmetry characterizations of Gaussianity, using Bell sampling on two copies for fermions and passive interferometry with photon counting on three copies for bosons. We further obtain tolerant testers requiring joint measurements on a larger, but still constant, number of copies. At the heart of our analysis is a unified approach---which we call the gradient-flow method---that applies across all structured families considered here and underlies our optimal testers: representation theory turns approximate satisfaction of the defining symmetry into quantitative control of the gradient of the rejection probability, allowing a continuous descent from the input state to the target family whose length bounds their distance.
summary: This paper develops optimal, resource-efficient quantum protocols to test if an unknown quantum state is Gaussian, applicable to both fermionic and bosonic systems. Using a novel gradient-flow method, the authors achieve a sample complexity independent of system size, making these tests highly scalable and experimentally feasible. This advances the field of quantum state characterization by providing robust, few-copy measurement schemes.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental and practical challenge of efficiently testing whether an unknown quantum state possesses the structure of a Gaussian state.
main_result: Optimal and robust algorithms are provided to test fermionic and bosonic Gaussianity with a sample complexity independent of the system size or particle number.
method: The authors develop a unified 'gradient-flow method' combining representation theory with the geometry of the rejection probability to derive these efficient, few-copy measurement protocols.
model_or_system: The focus is on pure fermionic and bosonic Gaussian states, which are central to quantum optics and many-body physics. Specific families include fermionic Gaussian states, general bosonic Gaussian states, and coherent states.
key_observables: Rejection probability $R(\psi)$, distance threshold $\epsilon$, and the required number of copies (sample complexity).
important_parameters: The sample complexity scales as $\Theta(\epsilon^{-2} \log(1/\delta))$, independent of the number of modes.
main_assumptions: The protocols are shown to be robust, meaning the measurement fidelity holds even when the state is slightly perturbed from the Gaussian family.
figures_summary: Figure 1 outlines the five target Gaussian families and the required copy numbers (two for fermions/some bosons, three for general bosons). Figure 2 details the operational measurements using Bell sampling for fermions and passive interferometry for bosons.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem, presents the unified gradient-flow method, derives the non-tolerant test complexity (Theorem II.1), and then extends to the more general, tolerant testing regime (Theorem II.2). Later sections detail the specific physical implementations for fermions and bosons.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous, resource-efficient quantum protocols for verifying fundamental structural properties (Gaussianity) in quantum states, which is crucial for validating simulations and understanding physical models in quantum optics and many-body physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Framework for robust few-copy Gaussianity testing. (a) We consider five target families of pure states: fermionic Gaussian states GF and their number-conserving subclass of Slater determinants S, as well as full bosonic Gaussian states G, centered Gaussian states G0, and coherent states C. Also shown a representations of Majorana fermions and cold fermionic atoms in optical lattices as typical physical architectures for fermions, and linear optical networks and cold bosonic in optical lattices as typical physical platforms for bosons. (b) Given identical copies of an unknown state vector ρψ = |ψ⟩⟨ψ|, the tests project onto a symmetry-defined acceptance subspace Kq. Two copies...

FIG. 2. Operational implementations of the few-copy Gaussianity tests. (a) Fermionic Gaussianity is tested on two copies by projecting onto the kernel of Λ = P2n µ=1 γµ ⊗γµ. Under a Jordan–Wigner encoding, this can be implemented by Bell measurements on corresponding orbital pairs, followed by linear-time classical post-processing. (b) General bosonic Gaussianity is tested on three copies. For each physical mode, a passive three-port interferometer separates the collective copy direction from two relative directions. After photon counting on the two relative output families, the test accepts iff their total photon numbers satisfy Nrel,+ = Nrel,−. The collective outputs are ignored.
